name: Smartsheet
tagline: Spreadsheet-shaped work management built on sheets, cell formulas, reports, and enterprise governance.
description: Smartsheet treats work as rows on a sheet, with cell formulas, Gantt views, reports, and Control Center governance for enterprise rollout.

content.title: Sheets, rows, and the grid you already know
content.body: Smartsheet's unit of work is a sheet: rows are items, columns are attributes, and the grid behaves like the spreadsheet most of its users already know. The enterprise guide in this repository records the product as combining familiar spreadsheet-like interfaces with project management capability, which is the whole adoption argument. People do not have to learn a new object model, only a new set of views over one they already use. That also explains why Smartsheet keeps appearing in this repository's enterprise, agency, and OKR lists: it is the standardization tool for organizations that already think in rows.

content.title: Gantt, critical path, and resource views
content.body: The same rows can be presented as a timeline. This repository records Smartsheet's project capabilities as Gantt charts, critical path analysis, and resource management, which is the layer separating a shared grid from a planning tool. Each view reads the underlying sheet, so a plan and its schedule cannot drift apart the way a separate document and tracker can. The surfaces below are what a buyer should ask to see during an evaluation, because their depth is what separates Smartsheet from a shared spreadsheet.
items: Gantt charts drawn from the sheet's dates
Critical path analysis across dependent rows
Resource views over assignments and capacity
Reports reading rows from several sheets
Control Center templates for repeated projects

content.title: Control Center and repeated project structures
content.body: For organizations running the same project shape many times, this repository records Smartsheet Control Center on the enterprise plan, described as a way to scale governance across multiple projects. The pattern matters more than the name: sheets are instantiated from a standard structure under central control, while teams keep editing at row level. Buyers weighing Smartsheet against single-project tools should ask whether repeatable deployment is what they are actually buying, because that is where the governance claim either holds or collapses into manual policing.

content.title: Where the grid stops helping
content.body: A spreadsheet model carries spreadsheet problems. Because structure lives in cells, sheets accumulate formulas, cross-sheet references, and hand-maintained conventions that only their original author understands, and cleanup becomes a project of its own. Grid semantics also ask teams to treat a task as a row: nested ownership, threaded discussion, and long documentation are weaker there than in a tool built around a task object. Neither issue is a defect, and both follow from choosing a grid. Teams that want the grid usually accept that trade consciously.

content.title: Two price records that do not line up
content.body: This page records Smartsheet as paid with a band of $7-25/mo, and no other figure appears here. A separate file in this repository places Smartsheet among enterprise platforms that start materially higher per user per month, which suggests the two records describe different tiers or different periods. Treat the band as indicative and ask the vendor for their current price list, particularly when budgeting a rollout across a whole PMO rather than a handful of sheets. The discrepancy is worth resolving before seat counts are agreed.

content.title: Admin controls, and the certifications not on file
content.body: Smartsheet is delivered as a hosted service, and the enterprise material in this repository records advanced admin and security controls on the enterprise plan without naming specific certifications. Our records hold no compliance certification entry for Smartsheet and this review will not assert one; read the current documentation the vendor publishes. For a grid holding plans across departments, the questions worth asking are about permission granularity at sheet and row level, audit history for structural changes, and where the underlying data resides.

content.title: Ten comparison pages, and what they argue about
content.body: This repository holds ten comparison pages featuring Smartsheet, and every one pairs it with another project tool: Airtable, Asana, Basecamp, ClickUp, Confluence, Jira, Linear, Monday.com, Trello, and Wrike. The recurring argument across those files is structure against flexibility, grids and governance on one side, task objects and boards on the other. The record also positions Smartsheet as the enterprise-side choice in several of these pairings, which is consistent with the tagline this page holds for it.

content.title: Smartsheet next to Basecamp, Wrike, and Jira
content.body: Basecamp, compared with Smartsheet on a page held in this repository, is the flat, opinionated alternative: no grid, no formulas, and communication built into a project instead of configuration. Wrike is the configurable middle, with request forms and reporting depth for teams that model their process first. Jira keeps appearing where agile rituals matter more than governed rows. Smartsheet wins when the requirement is a repeatable structure that non-technical departments can still edit, and loses when the requirement is fast setup or rich discussion attached to each item.

content.title: Who should standardize on Smartsheet
content.body: Smartsheet suits PMOs and operations groups that need one governed structure across many departments, and teams whose members already think in rows and formulas. It suits enterprises running repeated project shapes where Control Center-style governance is the actual requirement. It does not suit groups that want discussion, tasks, and files as first-class objects rather than cells, or buyers who need a single confirmed list price before signing. This assessment comes from published vendor material and the stored records this repository holds for Smartsheet; nothing here is based on operating the product. Those records show 4.3 out of 5 from 1,660 reviews.

faqs.question: Is Smartsheet a spreadsheet or a project tool?
faqs.answer: Both, by design. This repository records it as spreadsheet-like interfaces combined with project management capability, including Gantt charts, critical path analysis, and resource management over rows.

faqs.question: What is Smartsheet Control Center?
faqs.answer: The enterprise governance layer. This repository records it as scaling control across multiple projects, so sheets can be created from a standard structure while teams continue editing rows.

faqs.question: How does Smartsheet differ from Basecamp and Wrike?
faqs.answer: Basecamp is a fixed project container with message boards; Wrike is configurable, with request forms and reporting depth. Smartsheet is a governed grid where structure lives in cells and formulas.

faqs.question: How much does Smartsheet cost?
faqs.answer: This page's recorded band is $7-25/mo. A separate file in this repository places Smartsheet among enterprise platforms starting higher per user per month, so take list pricing straight from the vendor.

faqs.question: Does this repository record certifications for Smartsheet?
faqs.answer: No. It records advanced admin and security controls on the enterprise plan but stores no compliance certifications, so no such claim is made here and readers should confirm current documentation.

author: Sarah Chen
learningCurve: Moderate for authors: reading a sheet is instant, but building formulas, cross-sheet reports, and governance that other people can safely edit takes real setup
whoShouldUse: PMOs, operations groups, and enterprises that need a governed, repeatable structure across departments, and teams whose members are already comfortable in rows, columns, and formulas.
whoShouldNotUse: Groups that want tasks, threads, and documents as first-class objects rather than cells; teams that need fast setup without an administrator maintaining formulas; buyers who require a single confirmed price before procurement.
